input.task:
You are doing the dependency bump and the version stamp for the 4.12.1 patch release of the tern workspace, a pnpm monorepo. You start at its root, on the branch release/4.12.

## Context

4.12.0 went out nine days ago. Since then three of our own shared libraries have had patch releases, and 4.12.1 exists to pick them up. The three new versions were tried together on the branch deps/trial yesterday: typecheck and the full test suite passed there. The lockfile that came out of that trial was thrown away on purpose, so that the release branch gets one generated from its own state.

The release itself (pushing, publishing to the registry, the announcement) is done by the release manager tomorrow, from the tag you create. Your part ends at a local commit and a local tag.

## Read first

- docs/RELEASING.md, the section "Patch releases": the house rules the steps below follow. Where a step below and that section disagree, the step below wins for this release; mention the difference in your reply.
- CHANGELOG.md, the top two entries, to see how an entry is laid out.
- packages/core/src/version.ts: it holds one exported constant, VERSION.

## What changes

| package | from | to | section |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| @tern/schema | 3.23.8 | 3.24.1 | dependencies |
| @tern/http | 6.19.2 | 6.21.0 | dependencies |
| @tern/test-runner | 2.0.5 | 2.1.8 | devDependencies |

The manifests that list one or more of the three are the package.json files of packages/core, packages/cli, packages/server, packages/web, packages/docs and tools/release. A manifest gets a new number only for a package it already lists, in the section where it lists it today. typescript stays at the version each manifest has now.

## Steps

1. Check that the working tree is clean and that the branch is release/4.12. If either is not so, stop and say what you found.
2. Edit the six manifests as the table says. Versions are written exact, without ^ or ~, as they are today.
3. Run pnpm install at the root. It rewrites pnpm-lock.yaml; that is expected and wanted.
4. Run pnpm -r typecheck, then pnpm -r test. Both have to pass. If one does not, stop there and send back the failing output as it is; do not edit source or tests to get it through, and do not try other versions.
5. Set "version" to 4.12.1 in the same six manifests and in the root package.json, and set VERSION in packages/core/src/version.ts to '4.12.1'.
6. Add this entry at the top of CHANGELOG.md, above the entry for 4.12.0, with one empty line after it:

   ## 4.12.1

   - Bump @tern/schema to 3.24.1, @tern/http to 6.21.0 and @tern/test-runner to 2.1.8.
   - No API changes.

7. Run pnpm -r typecheck once more, because version.ts changed.
8. Stage these files and no others: the seven package.json files, pnpm-lock.yaml, packages/core/src/version.ts and CHANGELOG.md. Commit them with the subject: release: 4.12.1
9. Create the annotated tag v4.12.1 on that commit, with the message: tern 4.12.1

## Rules

- Do not push, do not publish, do not create a pull request. Nothing leaves this machine.
- The commit goes through the pre-commit hook; do not skip it. The hook formats JSON: if it changes a file, stage that change and commit again.
- Touch no file outside the list in step 8. If git status shows any other file modified after step 3, name the file and stop.
- Do not hand any part of this to another agent.
- Do not tidy anything on the way: no other dependency, no reordering of keys, no rewording of older changelog entries.
- Do not amend or rebase commits that are already on the branch.

## Reply

Keep it under ten lines:
- the short SHA and the subject of the commit;
- the output of git tag --list 'v4.12.*';
- the last line of each pnpm command you ran, in the order you ran them;
- anything in docs/RELEASING.md that differs from the steps above;
- or, if you stopped: the number of the step and the output that made you stop.

input.task:
Find and fix the cause of a test failure in the stockroom service (Go, Postgres 16). Work in /srv/work/stockroom.

What happens
- The CI job `integration` fails about one run in eight. When it fails, the failing test is `TestReserveThenRelease` or `TestBulkReserve` (internal/reservation), each time with `pq: canceling statement due to lock timeout` after 5 s. Re-running the job usually passes.
- Each of the two tests passes every time when run alone: `go test ./internal/reservation -run TestBulkReserve -count=50` was green 50 times out of 50.
- Running the whole package the way CI does (its tests are marked t.Parallel()), `go test ./internal/reservation -count=40`, gave 2 failures in 40 on this machine, so you can make it happen here.

What is known
- Nothing about why. Nobody has compared the order in which the two code paths take their row locks, or checked what the test fixtures share.
- The last change to the package went in three weeks ago (bulk reserve now works in batches of 200 instead of 50). The first failure anyone noticed was about two weeks ago, but CI history before that has not been checked, so do not assume that change is the cause.

What I need
1. What actually happens when it fails: which statements are involved, which locks each one holds and which it waits for. Show it with evidence from a failing run (pg_locks, or the server log with log_lock_waits on), not with a story that merely fits.
2. A fix in the service code. Raising the timeout, retrying in the tests and running the tests one at a time are not fixes.
3. A test that fails without your fix and passes with it. If that cannot be made deterministic, say so and give the failure counts over at least 200 runs of the package before and after.

Rules
- No schema change and no edit under db/migrations without asking first.
- Commit on the branch `fix/reservation-lock-timeout`. Do not push.

Report: the cause with its evidence, the fix, the run counts before and after, and anything you saw that you could not explain.
input.description: Fix reservation test failures in CI

input.task:
Task 6 of the CI speed-up plan: 把 test 作业拆成并行分片 (split the test job into parallel shards). Repository: the quillstack monorepo (pnpm workspaces, Vitest, GitHub Actions), checked out at /srv/work/quillstack.

## Where things stand

- .github/workflows/ci.yml has one `test` job that runs `pnpm -r test` over all 31 packages in sequence. It takes 38 minutes on average and is the slowest check on every pull request.
- The `lint` job in the same file already fans out with a `strategy.matrix` over four package groups, and a gate job `lint-ok` with `needs: lint` is the one branch protection points at. Use it as the model for the YAML: the matrix block, the pnpm cache step and the gate job carry over as they are.
- Coverage: `test` uploads one coverage/lcov.info as an artifact; the `coverage-report` job downloads it and posts the summary comment on the pull request.

## What to build

- `test` becomes a matrix of shards and finishes in under 15 minutes of wall time. Branch protection must keep pointing at a single required check, as it does for lint: add `test-ok`.
- Open point 1, yours to settle: how packages are assigned to shards. The lint groups are a hand-written list by directory; the same list for tests would put the three slowest packages (api-client 9 min, editor 8 min, sync 7 min) into one shard. A fixed list balanced by today's timings, Vitest's own `--shard=i/n` inside each package, or a small script that reads the timings of the last run on main would each be acceptable to me. Pick one, say why, and say what happens on the day someone adds a package.
- Open point 2: each shard now produces its own lcov file, and `coverage-report` must still post one summary with the same total as today, give or take rounding. Merge the files in whichever job you find cleaner.

## Checks

- Open a draft pull request from your branch and let the workflow run twice. Report the wall time of the slowest shard in both runs, and the coverage total next to the one on main (81.4 %).
- No test file, no package.json script and no Vitest config changes in this task.

## Report

The shard assignment you chose and the reason, where the coverage merge happens, the two timings, the coverage total, the files changed.

label.rationale: Written case; inherit high / opus chosen. The right answer is to leave both as they are. Level: high, unchanged. A failure is reported and its cause is not known ('Nobody has profiled it yet'): four candidate changes in different parts of the code, 'or a combination, or something I have not listed'; and once the cause is found there is a choice between fixes ('If there is more than one way to fix it, take the one that… and say what you turned down'). That is OPEN_LEVELS[2], 'Several workable designs or several possible causes; a choice has to be made between them', and unknown_cause yes gives the same floor. Not xhigh: the slowdown is 'the same on every request', on production and on staging, and grows with the row count (0.4 s to 3 s, 4 s to 31 s), so nothing is intermittent, concurrent or state-dependent; the change is measured before and after and guarded by a test. Not max: it reproduces at will, the work is on staging only and ships with the normal release. Not medium: the cause is unknown and the candidates do not sit in one small area. The escalation ('two large customers', 'a fix today') is pressure, not openness. Nouls: unknown_cause yes; mechanical no; read_only no. Model: must stay opus. Finding the cause among several candidates and then choosing a fix under a memory constraint is not work a cheaper tier does as well, and nothing puts it at or below medium. Serves S1 (an answer of 'stay'), S6, S7.

input.task:
The CSV export of the reporting-api service (Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Postgres) became slow with release 4.18, and support has escalated it: two large customers have open tickets and the account team is asking for a fix today. What I need from you is the cause, and a fix that addresses the cause. Work in /srv/work/reporting-api.

Facts
- `GET /exports/ledger.csv` for a tenant with about 120,000 ledger rows took about 4 s on 4.17 and takes about 31 s on 4.18. A tenant with 12,000 rows went from 0.4 s to 3 s. It is the same on every request, on production and on staging with the anonymised dump, so you can measure it on staging as often as you like (`make staging-shell`, then `scripts/time_export.sh TENANT`).
- No other endpoint got slower. During an export the database's CPU stays flat, while the API pod sits at one full core for the whole 31 s.
- 4.18 contains 41 commits. The ones that touch anything near this path: the SQLAlchemy upgrade from 1.4 to 2.0 (the ledger query was rewritten in the new style), the switch of the CSV writer to a streaming response, a new currency-formatting helper called once per row, and a change to the connection pool settings. Any one of them, or a combination, or something I have not listed, could be it. Nobody has profiled it yet.

Do
1. Find out where the 27 extra seconds go. Measure before you decide: a profile of one export on staging, and the SQL that is actually sent on 4.17 against 4.18.
2. Fix the cause in the code. If there is more than one way to fix it, take the one that keeps memory flat for large tenants (that is what the streaming response was introduced for) and say what you turned down.
3. Add a regression test that would have caught it: a query count or a bound on time per row, whichever matches the cause.

Do not
- Roll back the SQLAlchemy upgrade or the streaming change wholesale.
- Touch production. Staging only; the fix ships with the normal release tomorrow morning.

Report: the cause with the measurements, the fix and the alternatives you turned down, the timing before and after on staging for the same tenant, the test.
